title: Capstone Part 2: Deploy, Scale, and Operate
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 2: Deploy, Scale, and Operate ##### "Can I try it?" The most useful question anyone asks about a portfolio project, and the one most projects cannot survive. A hiring manager in Bengaluru described her filter: she opens the GitHub link, looks for a live URL, and clicks it. If it loads and works in under ten seconds, the candidate has demonstrated more than any notebook can. If there is no URL — or there is one and it 502s — she moves on. Yesterday you built a model that works on your machine. Today you make it a system that works for strangers, stays up when you are asleep, tells you when it degrades, and costs a defensible amount of money. That transition is the entire distinction between "did a project" and "shipped a product", and it is what senior interviews probe. ##### Optimise the model before you deploy it Deploying an unoptimised model wastes money at every subsequent step. ```python # Path A: transformer classifier -> ONNX + INT8 for CPU serving from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForSequenceClassification, ORTQuantizer from optimum.onnxruntime.configuration import AutoQuantizationConfig ort_model = ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("out/best", export=True) quantizer = ORTQuantizer.from_pretrained(ort_model) quantizer.quantize(save_dir="out/onnx-int8", quantization_config=AutoQuantizationConfig.avx512_vnni(is_static=False)) # Path B: LLM component -> vLLM with AWQ # python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model out/awq --quantization awq \ # --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --enable-prefix-caching --enable-chunked-prefill ``` Then measure and record the trade-off honestly: | Variant | Size | p50 | p95 | Macro-F1 | ₹/1k requests | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | PyTorch fp32, GPU | 1.1 GB | 24 ms | 41 ms | 0.834 | 4.80 | | ONNX fp32, CPU | 1.1 GB | 88 ms | 142 ms | 0.834 | 0.62 | | ONNX INT8, CPU | 280 MB | 31 ms | 54 ms | 0.829 | 0.24 | That table is a deliverable. It shows you can reason about cost, latency and quality together — and here it justifies serving on CPU at a twentieth of the price for 0.5 F1 points. ##### Containerise properly ```dockerfile # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7 FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest /uv /bin/uv WORKDIR /app COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \ uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project FROM python:3.12-slim RUN useradd -m -u 10001 app && apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /app COPY --from=builder /app/.venv /app/.venv COPY --chown=app:app src/ ./src/ COPY --chown=app:app models/onnx-int8/ ./models/ ENV PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH" \ PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \ OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 USER app EXPOSE 8000 HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=3s --start-period=90s \ CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/health || exit 1 CMD ["uvicorn", "src.api:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "2"] ``` Details that matter: a **multi-stage build** keeps the final image small; **non-root user** is a basic security control reviewers notice; **model weights baked into the image** make the container immutable and reproducible (fetch from object storage instead only if the model exceeds a few hundred MB); and `start-period=90s` gives the model time to load before health checks begin. ##### The service layer ```python from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, make_asgi_app import time, uuid, structlog log = structlog.get_logger() REQS = Counter("triage_requests_total", "", ["status", "category"]) LAT = Histogram("triage_latency_seconds", "", buckets=[.01,.025,.05,.1,.25,.5,1,2]) CONF = Histogram("triage_confidence", "", buckets=[.1,.3,.5,.7,.85,.95,1.0]) @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app: FastAPI): app.state.model = load_model("models/onnx-int8") app.state.version = MODEL_VERSION _ = app.state.model.predict(["warmup text"]) # warm the graph before ready yield app = FastAPI(title="Claim Triage", version=MODEL_VERSION, lifespan=lifespan) app.mount("/metrics", make_asgi_app()) class ClaimIn(BaseModel): description: str = Field(min_length=10, max_length=8000) product_code: str = Field(pattern=r"^[A-Z]{2}\d{4}$") claim_amount_inr: float = Field(ge=0, le=500_000) @app.get("/health") async def health(): return {"status": "ok", "model_version": app.state.version} @app.get("/ready") async def ready(request: Request): if not getattr(request.app.state, "model", None): raise HTTPException(503, "model not loaded") return {"status": "ready"} @app.post("/v1/triage") async def triage(claim: ClaimIn, request: Request): rid, t0 = str(uuid.uuid4()), time.perf_counter() text = redact_pii(claim.description) # DPDP: before inference and logs probs = request.app.state.model.predict_proba([text])[0] idx = int(probs.argmax()) category, conf = CATEGORIES[idx], float(probs[idx]) route = "human_review" if conf < THRESHOLDS[category] else "auto" dt = time.perf_counter() - t0 LAT.observe(dt); CONF.observe(conf); REQS.labels("ok", category).inc() log.info("prediction", request_id=rid, model_version=request.app.state.version, category=category, confidence=conf, route=route, latency_ms=dt * 1000, product_code=claim.product_code) return {"request_id": rid, "category": category, "confidence": conf, "route": route, "model_version": request.app.state.version} ``` The **confidence-based routing** is the design touch that shows product thinking: the system knows when it does not know, and defers to a human rather than guessing. Per-category thresholds tuned on validation data, not a global 0.5. ##### Kubernetes deployment ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: {name: claim-triage, namespace: capstone} spec: replicas: 2 selector: {matchLabels: {app: claim-triage}} template: metadata: labels: {app: claim-triage} annotations: {prometheus.io/scrape: "true", prometheus.io/port: "8000"} spec: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 containers: - name: api image: ghcr.io/you/claim-triage@sha256:9a1c... # digest, not tag resources: requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi} limits: {cpu: "2", memory: 3Gi} startupProbe: httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8000} failureThreshold: 30 periodSeconds: 5 readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8000}, periodSeconds: 5} livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}, periodSeconds: 20, failureThreshold: 5} lifecycle: preStop: {exec: {command: ["sleep", "10"]}} # drain before shutdown --- apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: {name: claim-triage} spec: scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: claim-triage} minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 10 metrics: - type: Resource resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 65}} behavior: scaleUp: {stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30} scaleDown: {stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300} --- apiVersion: policy/v1 kind: PodDisruptionBudget metadata: {name: claim-triage} spec: minAvailable: 1 selector: {matchLabels: {app: claim-triage}} ``` If Kubernetes is more than your project needs, that is a legitimate and defensible choice — Cloud Run, Fly.io or Railway with a documented rationale beats an over-engineered cluster. But package it as a Helm chart regardless, because that is what makes it portable and reviewable. ##### CI/CD with a safe rollout ```yaml name: deploy on: push: {branches: [main]} jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5 - run: uv sync --frozen - run: uv run ruff check src/ && uv run mypy src/ - run: uv run pytest tests/unit tests/data -q --cov=src --cov-fail-under=80 - run: uv run pytest tests/behavioural -q # directional + slice invariants model-gate: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: | uv run python -m scripts.validate_model \ --min-macro-f1 0.80 --min-worst-category-precision 0.72 \ --max-p95-latency-ms 120 --baseline-run "$BASELINE_RUN" build: needs: model-gate runs-on: ubuntu-latest outputs: {digest: "${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}"} steps: - id: push uses: docker/build-push-action@v6 with: {push: true, tags: "ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}"} - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master with: {image-ref: "ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}", exit-code: "1", severity: "CRITICAL,HIGH"} canary: needs: build runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: helm upgrade --install triage ./charts/triage -n capstone --atomic --set image.digest=${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }} --set canary.weight=10 - run: uv run python -m scripts.watch_canary --minutes 10 --max-error-rate 0.01 --max-p95-ms 150 --max-score-shift 0.03 - run: helm upgrade triage ./charts/triage -n capstone --set canary.weight=100 ``` `--atomic` plus a canary watcher gives you automated rollback. Demonstrating that in a demo — push a deliberately broken model, watch CI block it at the model gate, then push one that degrades at runtime and watch the canary revert it — is memorable in a way that a green checkmark is not. ##### Monitoring and drift ```mermaid flowchart TD A[API: structured prediction logs] --> B[(Log store / warehouse)] A --> P[Prometheus: latency, errors, confidence, cost] B --> D[Daily job: PSI per feature,
prediction distribution, data quality] D --> E[Evidently report + metrics] P --> G[Grafana dashboards] E --> G G --> AL{Alert rules} AL -->|P1| PG[Page: error rate, service down] AL -->|P2| TK[Ticket: PSI > 0.25 for 3 windows] AL -->|P3| DG[Weekly digest] B --> FB[Human review outcomes = delayed labels] FB --> PERF[Cohort performance with label coverage] PERF --> RT{Retrain trigger} ``` Build four dashboards, and screenshot them for your README: 1. **Service** — RPS, p50/p95/p99, error rate, replica count. 2. **Model** — prediction distribution by category, mean confidence, human-review rate, per-category volume. 3. **Drift** — PSI per feature, prediction drift, data-quality violations, days since retrain. 4. **Cost** — ₹ per request, daily spend, cost per resolved claim. Wire in the delayed-label loop: coordinators who override a routing decision are producing ground truth. Capture it, join it back on `request_id`, and compute cohort performance with label coverage reported alongside. ##### Load test and tune ```python # locustfile.py from locust import HttpUser, task, between import random class Coordinator(HttpUser): wait_time = between(1, 4) @task def triage(self): self.client.post("/v1/triage", json={ "description": random.choice(SAMPLE_CLAIMS), "product_code": random.choice(PRODUCT_CODES), "claim_amount_inr": random.uniform(500, 45_000), }, name="/v1/triage") ``` ```bash locust -f locustfile.py --headless -u 200 -r 20 -t 10m --host https://triage.example.in ``` Sweep concurrency, plot throughput against p95, and identify the knee. Record: maximum sustainable RPS per replica, the p95 at your target load, the replica count needed for projected 2,500 claims/day at a 4× peak factor, and the resulting monthly cost. Those four numbers turn "I deployed it" into "I sized it". ##### Documentation and demo Your README is the interface to everything above. Structure it as: a one-paragraph problem statement, a live demo link and a 90-second video, an architecture diagram, results with the honest table (including what you did *not* achieve), a "run it locally in three commands" section, and links to the design doc, model card and operational runbook. The **runbook** is the artifact almost nobody produces and everybody respects: ```markdown ## Runbook — Claim Triage Deploy: helm upgrade --install triage ./charts/triage -n capstone --atomic Rollback: helm rollback triage 0 -n capstone # measured TTR: 42 seconds Retrain: gh workflow run continuous-training.yml -f snapshot=YYYY-MM-DD Alerts P1 error_rate > 1% for 3m -> check /health, then rollback P1 p95 > 300ms for 5m -> check replica count and CPU throttling P2 PSI > 0.25 (3 windows) -> investigate upstream, consider retrain P2 human_review_rate > 25% -> confidence thresholds may need retuning Known issues - Hindi claims: F1 0.71 vs 0.86 English. Mitigation: routed to human below 0.9. - Cold start ~55s after scale-from-zero. minReplicas=2 avoids user impact. ``` Record the demo video. Show the live system, one deliberately ambiguous claim being routed to human review, the Grafana dashboard, and a rollback. Three minutes, no slides. ##### Common mistakes - Deploying an unoptimised model and paying 20× for inference. - No startup probe, so the pod is killed during model load. - `:latest` tags, making rollback impossible. - No load test, so capacity claims are guesses. - Logging predictions without the model version. - Raw PII in logs. - A global 0.5 confidence threshold instead of per-category values tuned on validation. - Dashboards that exist but are never screenshotted or shared. - No runbook, so the operational story is untold. - A dead demo link, which is worse than no demo link. ##### Hands-on Optimise, containerise and deploy your capstone with health, readiness and startup probes, structured logging including model version, Prometheus metrics, and autoscaling. Build the CI/CD pipeline with a model-validation gate and a canary rollout with automated rollback, then prove both work by deliberately pushing a regressed model. Load-test to find your knee point and record maximum sustainable RPS, p95 at target load, required replicas at projected scale, and monthly cost. For the mini-project, ship the complete capstone: a live, autoscaling, monitored deployment; four Grafana dashboards; drift detection with alerting; a delayed-label feedback loop; a cost and performance report with your optimisation table; a README with a working demo link and a three-minute video; a model card; and an operational runbook with a measured rollback time. Then write the operational documentation covering deployment, monitoring, alerting, rollback and cost — the runbook above is the shape, yours should be specific to your system and include the numbers you measured. ##### Key takeaways - Optimise before deploying — the accuracy/latency/cost table is itself a portfolio artifact. - Probes, non-root containers, pinned digests and graceful drain are what make a deployment reviewable. - A model-validation gate plus canary with automated rollback is the difference between shipping and gambling. - Monitor four planes — service, model, drift, cost — and close the loop with human-override labels. - The runbook, the load-test numbers and a working demo link are what turn a project into evidence of seniority.
